newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil reschedules CVRD auction to week's end.
newsitem.headline: Brazil reschedules CVRD auction to week's end.

text.p: Brazil rescheduled the auction of the state-owned mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) to the end of the week after failing on Wednesday to fend off legal challenges to the sale.

The privatisation of the world's largest iron ore producer now hinges on a decision by a judge at the Superior Court of Justice (STJ) who has to rule on a government appeal against a number of court injunctions blocking the sale.
"The auction is being called for Friday. We will be ready to carry out the auction as soon as the STJ makes a decision," Planning Minister Antonio Kandir told reporters.

Justice Democrito Ramos Reinaldo is due to consider whether it will accept the government appeal that all lawsuits against the CVRD sale across the country should be handled by a single tribunal because of a "conflict of interpretation" in lower courts.

Government officials had first rescheduled the auction, previously planned for April 29, for Wednesday, hoping that a favourable court decision would allow for the sell-off. But the STJ judge asked the government to provide in 10 days more information he deemed necessary before ruling on the appeal.
Kandir said the government would send all information to the justice by Friday morning in an attempt to get rid of all legal obstacles to CVRD's privatisation and kick off the sale.

More than 120 lawsuits have been filed against the company's privatisation, a record compared with the number of cases against the sell-off of steelmaker Usiminas, the first of Brazilian state companies to be privatised six years ago.
Earlier President Fernando Henrique Cardoso criticised the deluge of legal actions against the CVRD sale.
"I suppose we do live in the land of Carnival and it is good that people let their opinions be known but this is not the way forward," he said.

Seen as a key test to Cardoso's commitment to reform the economy, the sale of CVRD, considered the biggest in Latin America to date, has mobilised considerable opposition from nationalists and leftists.
Opponents, from former presidents Itamar Franco and Jose Sarney to Brazil's Roman Catholic bishops, have accused the government of selling the country's mineral wealth to foreigners for a pittance.
The company's Carajas mine is the biggest iron ore deposit in the world with reserves of 15 billion tonnes.

With the sale of a maximum 45 percent voting stake in CVRD mining conglomerate, the government expects to net at least $2.8 billion. If completed, the firm's privatisation could net the government about $5.0 billion.

Two groups are ready to bid for the control of the miner: one led by local steel firm CSN, and another headed by Brazil's largest private industrial conglomerate Grupo Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
Both are confident that the government will win the legal battles surrounding the CVRD privatisation.
